quotes.t: Cherish that which is within you, and shut off that which is without; for much knowledge is a curse.
Forget the years, forget distinctions. Leap into the boundless and make it your home!
Great wisdom is generous; petty wisdom is contentious. Great speech is impassioned, small speech cantankerous.
I do not know whether I was then a man dreaming I was a butterfly, or whether I am now a butterfly dreaming I am a man.
Rewards and punishments are the lowest form of education.

Right is not right; so is not so. If right were really right, it would differ so clearly from not right that there would be no need for argument. If so were really so, it would differ so clearly from not so that there would be no need for argument. Forget the years; forget distinctions. Leap into the boundless and make it your home!
quotes.c: Zhuangzi, Ch. 2 (tr. Burton Watson, 1968) If right were really right, it would be so different from not-right that there would be no room for argument. If so were really so, then it would be so different from not-so that there would be no room for argument. Tr. Paul Kjellberg, in Readings in Classical Chinese Philosophy (2001) ch. 5, p. 224

quotes.t: Those who seek to satisfy the mind of man by hampering it with ceremonies and music and affecting charity and devotion have lost their original nature.
We cling to our own point of view, as though everything depended on it. Yet our opinions have no permanence; like autumn and winter, they gradually pass away.
quotes.c: Zhuangzi, Ch. 2 (tr. Gia-Fu Feng and Jane English, 1974)

quotes.t: All men know the utility of useful things; but they do not know the utility of futility.
Away then with wisdom and knowledge, and great robbers will disappear!

For all men strive to grasp what they do not know, while none strive to grasp what they already know; and all strive to discredit what they do not excel in, while none strive to discredit what they do excel in. This is why there is chaos.

Great truths do not take hold of the hearts of the masses...And now, as all the world is in error, I, though I know the true path,-how shall I guide? If I know that I cannot succeed and yet try to force success, this would be but another source of error. Better, then, to desist and strive no more. But if I strive not, who will?
He who knows what is of God and who knows what is of Man has reached indeed the height (of wisdom).
He who pursues fame at the risk of losing his self is not a scholar.

Once upon a time, I, Chuang Chou, dreamt I was a butterfly, fluttering hither and thither, to all intents and purposes a butterfly. I was conscious only of my happiness as a butterfly, unaware that I was Chou. Soon I awaked, and there I was, veritably myself again. Now I do not know whether I was then a man dreaming I was a butterfly, or whether I am now a butterfly, dreaming I am a man. Between a man and a butterfly there is necessarily a distinction. The transition is called the transformation of material things.
Perfect happiness is keeping yourself alive, and only actionless action can have this affect.
quotes.c: Zhuangzi, Ch. 18 (tr. Martin Palmer and Elizabeth Breuily, 1996)

quotes.t: Resolve your mental energy into abstraction, your physical energy into inaction. Allow yourself to fall in with the natural order of phenomena, without admitting the element of self,-and the empire will be governed.

The fish trap exists because of the fish; when you've got the fish, you can forget the trap. The rabbit snare exists because of the rabbit; once you've got the rabbit, you can forget the snare. Words exist because of meaning; once you've got the meaning, you can forget the words. Where can I find a man who has forgotten words so I can have a word with him?

The great bird rises on the wind to a height of a thousand miles. What does it see from on high there in the blue? Is it droves of wild horses galloping? Is it primeval matter whirling in atomic dust? Is it the exhalations that give birth to all things? Is it the blue of the sky itself, or is it only the colour of infinite distance?
quotes.c: Zhuangzi, Ch. 1 (tr. Anthony Watson-Gandy and Terence Gordon, from the French of René Grousset, 1952)

quotes.t: Those in positions of power spend day and night plotting and pondering about what to do. The body is treated in a very careless way. People live their lives, constantly surrounded by anxiety. If they live long before dying, they end up in senility, worn out by concerns: a terrible fate.
quotes.c: Zhuangzi, Ch. 18 (tr. Martin Palmer and Elizabeth Breuily, 1996)

quotes.t: Thus, the wise man looks into space, and does not regard the small as too little, nor the great as too much; for he knows that there is no limit to dimension.
quotes.c: Zhuangzi, Ch. 17 莊子/秋水 (tr. Herbert A. Giles, 1889)

quotes.t: To know to stop where they cannot arrive by means of knowledge is the highest attainment. Those who cannot do this will be destroyed on the lathe of Heaven.
You cannot speak of ocean to a well-frog.
quotes.c: Zhuangzi, Ch. 17 莊子/秋水 (tr. Herbert A. Giles, 1889) Of a person who has limited life experience and hence world view; see 井底之蛙

quotes.t: 昔者庄周梦为蝴蝶，栩栩然蝴蝶也，自喻适志与，不知周也。俄然觉，则戚戚然周也。不知周之梦为蝴蝶与，蝴蝶之梦为周与？周与蝴蝶则必有分矣。此之谓物化。
Happiness is the absence of the striving for happiness.
When deeds and words are in accord, the whole world is transformed.
Flow with whatever is happening and let your mind be free. Stay centered by accepting whatever you are doing. This is the ultimate.
Life is really simple, but we insist on making it complicated.
The perfect man employs his mind as a mirror. It does not lean for or against anything. It responds to things but conceals no traces; then, like a perfect balance, it is empty.
The perfect man uses his mind as a mirror. It does not lean forward or backward in its responses.
The sage does not seek to be famous. He is content to be unknown.
The sage does not seek to be first. He is content to be last.
The sage does not seek to be free. He is content to be bound.
The sage does not seek to be great, and therefore he is great.
The sage does not seek to be loved. He is content to be hated.
The sage does not seek to be perfect. He is content to be imperfect.
The sage does not seek to be wise. He is content to be a fool.
The sage has no fixed ideas. He is the mirror of the people.
The sage is like a mirror, reflecting all things but not holding onto any.
The sage is like an infant, his mind is not yet confused with the distinctions of good and bad.
The sage is like the earth, supporting all things, and giving life to all things.
The sage is like the frost, covering all things, and bringing beauty to the world.
The sage is like the great happiness, which is hidden in all things and is not seen.
The sage is like the moon, which waxes and wanes but never changes its nature.
The sage is like the sky at dawn, which is clear on all sides.
The sage is like the tortoise, who carries his home on his back, and is never without shelter.
The sage is like the uncarved block, which can be made into anything.
The sage is like the valley, receiving all things and giving nothing back.
The sage is like the valley, which receives all things and is never full.
The sage is like the water, flowing always downward, and seeking the lowest place.
The sage is like the water, which benefits all things and contends with none.
The sage is like the wind, blowing always onward, and seeking the farthest place.
The sage is like the wind, he does not strive to be strong or weak, but simply follows his course.
The sage is like the wind, which blows on all things without partiality.
The wise man does not hoard. The more he gives to others, the more he has himself.
The wise man does not lay up his own ideas. He is from whom the people learn. He who is self-displaying in his learning cannot enlighten the people.
The wise man does not lay up his own opinions about anything, nor does he anoint himself with his own praises.
The wise man does not seek to be enlightened. He is content to be ignorant.
The wise man does not seek to be great. He is content to be small.
The wise man does not seek to be powerful. He is content to be powerless.
The wise man does not seek to be praised. He is content to be blamed.
The wise man does not seek to be rich. He is content with what he has.
The wise man is like a mirror, he does not lean forward or backward in his response to things.
The wise man is like an infant, drifting with the currents, changing at the seasons.
The wise man is like the fire, burning always upward, and seeking the highest place.
The wise man is like the moon, he does not strive to be full or new, but simply follows his course.
The wise man is like the river, flowing always onward, and never resting in one place.
The wise man is like the sky, covering all things, and protecting all things.
The wise man is like the stars, guiding travelers in the night, and bringing hope to the world.
The wise man is like the sun, shining on all things, and bringing light to the world.
The wise man is like the wind, blowing where it will, and not bound by any one place.
The wise man is never elated, never depressed; he is never carried away by the passing mood.
The wise man is not afraid of death. He knows that it is a natural part of life.
The wise man is not afraid of solitude. He finds companionship in nature and the universe.
The wise man is not attached to his own identity. He knows that the self is an illusion.
The wise man is not attached to his own opinions. He is open to new ideas and perspectives.
The wise man is not attached to material possessions. He knows that they are impermanent.
The wise man is not bound by social conventions. He follows his own inner guidance.
The wise man is not bound by the limitations of the mind. He transcends thought.
The wise man is not concerned with fame or fortune. He seeks only to live in harmony with the Tao.
The wise man is not confined by his knowledge. He is open to all things.
The wise man is not confined by physical boundaries. He is free to roam the universe.
The wise man is not disturbed by external events. He remains calm and centered.
The wise man is not swayed by the opinions of others. He follows his own path.
The wise man is not the one who gives the right answers, but the one who poses the right questions.
The wise man is not the one who has all the answers, but the one who knows where to find them.
The wise man is not the one who is never afraid, but the one who knows how to conquer fear.
The wise man is not the one who is never angry, but the one who knows how to control anger.
The wise man is not the one who is never in danger, but the one who knows how to face danger.
The wise man is not the one who is never in doubt, but the one who knows how to seek the truth.
The wise man is not the one who is never in error, but the one who knows how to correct his errors.
The wise man is not the one who is never in pain, but the one who knows how to endure.
The wise man is not the one who is never in the dark, but the one who knows how to find the light.
The wise man is not the one who is never in want, but the one who knows how to live without.
The wise man is not the one who is never sad, but the one who knows how to overcome sadness.
The wise man is not the one who is never tired, but the one who knows how to rest.
The wise man is not the one who knows much, but the one who loves much.
The world is impermanent, and so is life. To understand this is to be enlightened.
